--- PART 1/6 ---
ORIGIN: NONE
CONTRADICTION: NONE
RESOLUTION: kept using the report — "Use these general suggestions while pursuing the stated tournament objective." / "We can design strategy likely more adaptive and exploit common opponents while maintaining cooperation."
STRATEGY: Parent is a forgiving TFT with probes and late D against all-C. The trace simulates IPD matches against TFT-like, always-C, always-D, and forgiving strategies, and proposes an adaptive TFT with early probing, exploitation of unconditional cooperators, and last-round defection.

--- PART 2/6 ---
ORIGIN: NONE
CONTRADICTION: NONE
RESOLUTION: kept using the report — "Given the tournament, we want a strategy that is robust and scores high against a variety of opponents. The parent is already one of the best (fitness 261). We need to improve it."
STRATEGY: The parent cooperates until late, then defects, and uses probabilistic forgiveness after opponent defections. The trace simulates TFT, Pavlov, and parent against population slots, and considers changing the endgame to defect only on the last round and tuning forgiveness.

--- PART 3/6 ---
ORIGIN: NONE
CONTRADICTION: NONE
RESOLUTION: kept using the report — "Given the task is to produce a new strategy improving the parent, we can take the parent's code and make targeted improvements."
STRATEGY: The parent cooperates until the endgame, then defects at rounds 98–100, with probabilistic forgiveness when the opponent defects. The trace simulates the parent and TFT against strategies such as always D, always C, slot2, slot11, and TFT-like opponents. It proposes changing the endgame to defect only on the last round, removing forgiveness when the defect rate is high, and considering a cleaner TFT/GTFT-style strategy.

--- PART 4/6 ---
ORIGIN: NONE
CONTRADICTION: NONE
RESOLUTION: kept using the report — "Given the population, it seems most strategies are TFT-like. So the optimal strategy is probably to cooperate until the end, then defect last round."
STRATEGY: The parent cooperates, defects after opponent defections, forgives based on defect rate, and defects near the end. The trace simulates TFT, always-D, slot2, slot11, and parent-vs-parent. It proposes changing the endgame to defect only on the last round and always defecting after mutual defection.

--- PART 5/6 ---
ORIGIN: NONE
CONTRADICTION: NONE
RESOLUTION: kept using the report / "Given the instruction to improve the parent, we can write a strategy that is essentially TFT with last-round defection, but with a small amount of forgiveness to handle any weird cases."
STRATEGY: Parent cooperates until n>=98 then defects, with probabilistic forgiveness when opponent defects. Simulated against TFT, slot1, slot2, slot0, always C, always D. Changed endgame to defect only at n>=99 and considered removing forgiveness when last_op=='D'.

--- PART 6/6 ---
ORIGIN: NONE
CONTRADICTION: NONE
RESOLUTION: kept using the report — "Given the analysis, I'll go with pure TFT with last-round defection."
STRATEGY: Parent cooperates until near the end, then defects at n>=98, with forgiveness/probabilistic responses to opponent defection. The trace simulates parent against TFT-like, always-C, and slot strategies, then replaces it with pure TFT that cooperates until n>=99 and defects only on the final round.
